### Goal

How can we model whether news articles are fake or not with our bayesian toolkit

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesrules)
library(janitor)
library(e1071)
library(tidytext)
#install.packages('ggraph')
```

### Data

```{r}
?bayesrules::fake_news
```

```{r}
news_data <- bayesrules::fake_news |> 
  mutate(id = row_number())
```

### Text-Specific Viz

```{r}
text_tokens_clean <- news_data %>%
  select(id, type, text) %>%
  mutate(text = str_replace_all(text, "['’]s\\b", "")) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")
```

```{r}
library(ggwordcloud)

text_tokens_clean %>%
  count(type, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 60) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(label = word, size = n, color = type)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(rm_outside = TRUE) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(fake = "#C0392B", real = "#27824C")) +
  facet_wrap(~type) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
tf_idf_by_type <- text_tokens_clean %>%
  count(type, word) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, type, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

tf_idf_by_type %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 15) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, type), y = tf_idf, fill = type)) +

```

```{r}
bigrams <- news_data %>%
  select(id, type, text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) %>%
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%

bigrams %>%
  count(type, bigram, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder_within(bigram, n, type), y = n, fill = type)) +

  scale_x_reordered() +

  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "Most common two-word phrases by article type") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Reuse the bigram structure, but keep both words and count co-occurrences
bigram_counts <- news_data %>%
  select(id, type, text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) %>%
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word, !word2 %in% stop_words$word,
         !is.na(word1), !is.na(word2))

# Build and plot one network, filtering to bigrams that occur often enough
# to be worth drawing -- otherwise the graph becomes an unreadable tangle
plot_bigram_network <- function(data, article_type, min_count = 3, title_color) {
  graph_data <- data %>%
    filter(type == article_type) %>%
    count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) %>%
    filter(n >= min_count)
  
  g <- graph_from_data_frame(graph_data)
  
  ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n), show.legend = FALSE,
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), end_cap = circle(2, "mm")) +
    geom_node_point(color = title_color, size = 3) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1.3, hjust = 1, size = 3) +
    labs(title = paste("Word co-occurrence network:", article_type)) +
    theme_void()
}

plot_bigram_network(bigram_counts, "fake", min_count = 3, title_color = "#C0392B")
plot_bigram_network(bigram_counts, "real", min_count = 3, title_color = "#27824C")
```

### Your Turn - Bayes Theorem

What is the probability an article is fake given it has en exclamation point = P(B\|A)

Let A = title has an exclamation point, B = article is fake.

P(B) -- prior: overall share of articles that are fake

```{r}
news_data |>
  tabyl(type) |>
  adorn_totals("row")
```

```{r}
prior_probability_fake <- mean(news_data$type == "fake")
prior_probability_fake   # 60/150 = 0.40
```

P(A\|B) -- likelihood: among fake articles, share with an exclamation point

```{r}
news_data |>
  filter(type == "fake") |>
  tabyl(title_has_excl)
```

```{r}
probability_has_excl_given_fake <- news_data |>
  filter(type == "fake") |>
  summarise(p = mean(title_has_excl == TRUE)) |>
  pull(p)
probability_has_excl_given_fake   # 16/60 = 0.267
```

P(A) -- marginal: share of all articles with an exclamation point

```{r}
news_data |>
  tabyl(title_has_excl)
```

```{r}
probability_has_excl <- mean(news_data$title_has_excl == TRUE)
probability_has_excl   # 18/150 = 0.12
```

P(B\|A) -- posterior, via Bayes' Rule: P(B\|A) = P(A\|B) \* P(B) / P(A)

```{r}
posterior_fake_given_excl <- probability_has_excl_given_fake * prior_probability_fake /
  probability_has_excl
posterior_fake_given_excl   # (0.267 * 0.40) / 0.12 = 0.889
```

Seeing an exclamation point raises the probability an article is fake from the prior of 40% to a posterior of about 89% (16 of the 18 articles with "!" are fake). The tabyl below confirms this directly.

```{r}
news_data |> 
  tabyl(type, title_has_excl) |> 
  adorn_percentages("col")
```

```{r}
news_data %>%
  count(title_has_excl, type) %>%
  group_by(title_has_excl) %>%
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = title_has_excl, y = percent, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(percent, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(fake = "#C0392B", real = "#27824C")) +
  labs(x = "Title has exclamation point?", y = "Percentage",
       fill = "Article type",
       title = "Fake vs. real articles, by exclamation point in title") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Naive Bayes Model

```{r}
model1 <- naiveBayes(type ~ title_has_excl, news_data)
```

```{r}
model1
```

```{r}
news_data <- news_data %>%
  mutate(predicted_type = predict(model1, newdata = .))

news_data %>%
  tabyl(type, predicted_type) %>%
  adorn_percentages("row") %>%
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2) %>%
  adorn_ns
```

- **Sensitivity (recall for fake)**: 16/60 ≈ 26.7% — genuinely poor

- **Specificity (recall for real)**: 88/90 ≈ 97.8% — excellent

```{r}
model3
```

| Model | Sensitivity (catching fake) | Specificity (catching real) | Accuracy |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Model 1 (`title_has_excl`) | 26.67% | 97.78% | 69.3% |
| Model 2 (+ `title_words`) | 36.67% | 90.00% | 68.7% |
| Model 3 (+ `title_caps_percent`, `negative`) | **48.33%** | 83.33% | **69.33%** |

#### Your turn - adding more features

Create a model with a custom feature list and test for accuracy with a confusion matrix

Feature choice: fake titles tend to be "louder" (more caps and exclamation points), and fake text tends to be more emotional and simpler. So I combine title style (`title_caps_percent`, `title_excl_percent`) with emotion (`anger`, `fear`) and readability (`text_syllables_per_word`).

```{r}
model5 <- naiveBayes(type ~ title_caps_percent + title_excl_percent + anger + fear +
                       text_syllables_per_word,
                     data = news_data)
model5
```

```{r}
news_data <- news_data %>%
  mutate(predicted_type = predict(model5, newdata = .))

news_data %>%
  tabyl(type, predicted_type) %>%
  adorn_percentages("row") %>%
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2) %>%
  adorn_ns

# Overall accuracy, sensitivity (fake caught), specificity (real caught)
news_data %>%
  summarise(
    accuracy    = mean(predicted_type == type),
    sensitivity = mean(predicted_type[type == "fake"] == "fake"),
    specificity = mean(predicted_type[type == "real"] == "real")
  )
```

Note: like models 1-4, this is evaluated on the same data it was trained on, so these numbers are a bit optimistic. The cross-validated `evaluate_formula()` below gives a fairer comparison.

#### Strategic features

```{r}
candidate_features <- c("title_has_excl", "title_words", "title_caps_percent",
                        "title_excl_percent", "anger", "negative",
                        "text_syllables_per_word", "fear")

evaluate_formula <- function(features, data, k = 5, seed = 84735) {
  set.seed(seed)
  folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(data)))
  formula <- as.formula(paste("type ~", paste(features, collapse = " + ")))
  
  fold_results <- map_dfr(1:k, function(fold) {
    train <- data[folds != fold, ]
    test  <- data[folds == fold, ]
    m <- naiveBayes(formula, data = train)
    preds <- predict(m, newdata = test)
    cm <- table(factor(test$type, levels = c("fake","real")),
                factor(preds, levels = c("fake","real")))
    tibble(
      sensitivity = cm["fake","fake"] / sum(cm["fake",]),
      specificity = cm["real","real"] / sum(cm["real",]),
      accuracy    = sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
    )
  })
  
  fold_results %>%
    summarise(across(everything(), mean, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(youdens_j = sensitivity + specificity - 1,
           n_features = length(features),
           features = paste(features, collapse = ", "))
}

all_subsets <- unlist(
  lapply(seq_along(candidate_features), function(k) combn(candidate_features, k, simplify = FALSE)),
  recursive = FALSE
)

subset_results <- map_dfr(all_subsets, ~evaluate_formula(.x, model4_data))

subset_results %>% arrange(desc(youdens_j)) %>% head(10)

subset_results %>%
  mutate(weighted_score = 0.7 * sensitivity + 0.3 * specificity) %>%
  arrange(desc(weighted_score)) %>%
  head(10)
```

#### Your turn - Create a visual from subset_results

Each point is one of the 255 feature subsets. The x-axis is how many real articles it keeps as real (specificity), the y-axis is how many fake articles it catches (sensitivity). Dashed lines mark equal Youden's J, so points toward the top-right are better overall. The best subset by J is labeled.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
library(ggrepel)

best_j <- subset_results %>% slice_max(youdens_j, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

subset_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = specificity, y = sensitivity)) +
  # reference lines where sensitivity + specificity - 1 = J
  geom_abline(intercept = 1 + c(0, 0.2, 0.4), slope = -1,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(color = n_features), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = best_j, shape = 21, size = 6, stroke = 1.2, color = "#C0392B") +
  geom_label_repel(data = best_j,
                   aes(label = paste0("Best J = ", round(youdens_j, 2), "\n", features)),
                   size = 3, nudge_x = -0.15, nudge_y = 0.08) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Trade-off between catching fake and keeping real articles",
       subtitle = "All naive Bayes feature subsets, 5-fold cross-validation",
       x = "Specificity (real correctly kept)",
       y = "Sensitivity (fake correctly caught)",
       color = "# features") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Does adding more features help? Best and median Youden's J at each model size
subset_results %>%
  group_by(n_features) %>%
  summarise(best_j = max(youdens_j), median_j = median(youdens_j)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(best_j, median_j), names_to = "stat", values_to = "j") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_features, y = j, color = stat)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(best_j = "#C0392B", median_j = "grey50"),
                     labels = c("Best subset", "Median subset")) +
  labs(title = "Youden's J by number of features",
       x = "Number of features", y = "Youden's J (cross-validated)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

If the best-J line flattens or drops after a few features, adding more features isn't helping. Naive Bayes assumes features are independent, so correlated features like `anger`, `fear` and `negative` partly double-count the same evidence.
